item.title: Mao Zedong and the founding of the People's Republic of China (2/3) | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
From peasants' son to revolutionary leader — Mao Zedong laid the foundation for modern China. This three-part documentary offers an in-depth look at one of the most influential figures of the 20th century. *Part 3 coming soon!*
Part 1: https://youtu.be/dP8dX4Pyzd0 Part 2: https://youtu.be/kml_5jNV0j8 Part 3: Available from 17 October 2026
The legacy of the "founding father" of the People's Republic of China remains deeply controversial. Revered in Europe as a revolutionary icon in the late 1960s, Mao led China to the brink of disaster and ultimately clung to power with a regime of terror. Yet today's leaders in Beijing continue to draw on the cult of Mao. China is now a global power, a transformation that would be difficult to imagine without Mao Zedong.
When Mao Zedong was born in 1893, nothing hinted at his meteoric rise to power. The son of a farming family, he grew up during a period of political instability and profound social upheaval. The 1911 Revolution, which marked the beginning of the end of imperial rule, awakened his mind to politics. At first, Mao had no clear political program. But the Russian Revolution of 1917 introduced him to Marxist ideas, and he soon became a co-founder of the Communist Party of China.
Mao rose steadily through the party ranks as conflict with the nationalist Kuomintang party intensified into a bloody civil war. The devastating retreat that became known as the "Long March" went down in history to become the foundation of the cult of Mao. After World War II, the struggle for power in China continued until Mao and his forces finally reached Beijing.
This three-part series traces Mao Zedong's journey from peasants' son to revolutionary and architect of modern China — from his rural childhood to the founding of the People's Republic to the devastating impact of the Cultural Revolution in the 1960s, which claimed millions of lives.
Archival footage, as well as interviews with historians and eyewitnesses, tell the story of the man who changed China forever.

item.title: Skin: Multitalented and underappreciated | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Our skin connects us to the world while also providing us with a boundary and a layer of protection. It's a biotope, an object of desire, and it allows us to smell the way we do. How can we keep our skin healthy, and heal it when it's unwell?
On average, the skin is around two square meters in area and weighs between five and ten kilograms. For a long time, it was viewed primarily as a covering. But this multitalented organ is much more than that. It provides us with one of our senses, it can draw oxygen directly from the air, and it can even perceive sound waves and odor molecules.
The skin is also a status symbol, with smooth, wrinkle-free skin symbolizing youth, beauty and success. Countless experts offer advice, including recommending anti-aging products containing acids, bases, enzymes, vitamins, or proteins. But only a few cosmetics are truly worth it, says dermatologist Professor Claudia Borelli of the University Hospital in Tübingen, Germany. The same goes for the advice of many skincare influencers, who often promote their own interests on social media. So is it better to think twice before rushing to get cosmetic treatments?
Over the past five years, procedures using Botox and hyaluronic acid have more than doubled. Borelli warns that poorly administered fillers can cause problems for years to come. Nevertheless, the clients of cosmetic doctors are getting younger and younger. Gaming streamer Jasmin Gnu had lip fillers in her early 20s — she now regrets that decision. She tells her fans that they don't have to chase the unattainable aesthetic ideals sold to them by the beauty filters used on social media.
Meanwhile, the skin can also be seen as a window into the soul. Stress can make the skin sick, says psychodermatologist Professor Uwe Gieler. About a quarter of Germans suffer from skin conditions such as atopic dermatitis, psoriasis, acne, or allergies. With the help of an anti-inflammatory diet, new medications and therapy, there's a good chance of healing unhealthy skin.

DESCRIPTION Garrison Hinson-Hasty, author of “Systems Programming with Zig” and a contributor to the Zig compiler, joins Trevor Berrange Sanchez to explain why he wrote a book on a pre-1.0 language that breaks frequently (he's currently updating the last seven chapters for Zig 0.16). His answer: the language's slow march toward 1.0 is a feature, and learning it now teaches you why its decisions stick. The conversation's core thesis is that Zig is countercultural: instead of stacking new abstractions on old ones, it reuses well-tested ideas and "never adds too much”. "Simple", in the Zig community's sense, means simple relative to what the machine is doing, with integer and pointer types that map closely to how you'd think about data in assembly. Chapter 6's CHIP-8 interpreter shows this: a few integers, some buffers, and elegant results. The same philosophy explains Zig's missing string type. Strings are just byte sequences with a length, and the language leaves encoding choices to you. Garrison notes that Rust, by contrast, now has to maintain its many string types forever.
Two practical takeaways for working engineers. First, allocators: because Zig encourages flat, data-oriented design, the book barely needs dynamic allocation, and when it does, allocators let you reason about memory for a whole phase of a program (say, a compiler's parser) as one unit rather than tracking the lifetime of every AST node. Second, C interop: you can use a C header directly, keep defer for cleanup instead of goto, and write small Zig wrappers around awkward C error-return conventions. The chapter on graphics and OpenGL, meanwhile, is really about a transferable systems skill: working out what an unfamiliar, committee-designed API wants from you when no tutorial exists.

item.title: Through Kazakhstan by train | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Each year, a train carrying doctors and medical gear travels through remote areas of Kazakhstan. The project is called Salamatty Kazakhstan, or "Healthy Kazakhstan." The train is underway for eight months and the clinic operates daily.
Salamatty Kazakhstan was launched by the government to improve medical care in the country's sparsely populated regions. Some communities are hundreds of kilometers from the nearest hospital or clinic. The train's timetable is shared online.
In addition to medical staff, the train crew includes kitchen staff, stewards, and technicians. On its journey of around 20,000 kilometers, the train stops in numerous villages and small towns in the Kazakh countryside. The film follows this unique social project, showing doctors and support staff as they form close bonds during the eight-month journey: working, eating and living together. Patients come to the clinic with physical ailments, but they also share their everyday worries.
The film offers a rare glimpse into this oil-rich Central Asian country. It gives viewers a sense of the respect and dedication at the heart of these special encounters between two very different worlds.

item.title: From 0 to 9 - The mysterious origins of our numbers | DW Documentary
item.author: DW Documentary
item.content:encoded:
Why do people in Europe refer to them as "Arabic numerals" when they were invented in India? How could ten tiny symbols conquer the world? And how did zero change the course of history?
The Western world calls them "Arabic numerals," while in the Arab world, today's European notation is thought of as being Western. What is "Arabic" about the symbols that traveled from India to Europe and on to the rest of the world?
Following the trail of our numbers leads us to Baghdad. There, in the eighth century, a scholar named al-Khwarizmi — Latinized as "Algorismi," later to be found in the word "algorithm" — helped spread Indian numerals. He would become known as the father of modern algebra. The "Arabic" numerals commonly used in Europe today derive from another variant, known as "Ghubar" — Arabic for "dust." That had emerged from the so-called "dust tables" used by Maghrebi merchants around the Mediterranean.
From Europe to America, and from the dawn of modern science to the computer age — the fascinating history of these ten small digits is enmeshed with the stories of the people who invented, spread, adopted, imposed and scrutinized them. Little by little, they have permeated every area of our lives. With the computer, numbers became the code of the modern age — and the only truly universal language.

Melting glaciers, rising sea levels, fires, floods and droughts: In 2008, with public concern about global warming on the upswing, award-winning producer and correspondent Martin Smith traveled the planet to investigate the scale of the problem, and the scale of any solution.
For years, the film reported, big businesses in the U.S. and around the globe — from oil and coal companies to electric utilities to car manufacturers — had resisted change to environmental policy and stifled the debate over climate change. But as this 2008 documentary was being made, industries and governments were facing rising pressure to reshape their approach to the environment.
To make “Heat,” Smith traveled to 12 countries on four continents, sitting down with policymakers, scientists, and leading executives from many of the largest carbon emitters from around the world, including American oil giants, Chinese coal companies, and Indian SUV makers.
The two-hour film documented where the political and economic conversation around climate change and global warming stood in 2008, and found that some businesses were trying to fend off new regulations, while others were repositioning themselves to prosper in a world reshaped by climate change. The investigation also found that despite increasing talk about “going green,” environmental concerns were often still taking a back seat to shorter-term economic interests. And there were serious questions about the ability of industry-proposed solutions like “clean coal,” ethanol fuel subsidies, and carbon capture technology to roll back global warming.
Editor’s note: A line of narration in this documentary cited a since-retracted assertion from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change that "80 percent of all glacier ice in Tibet and the Himalayas will be gone by 2035." The panel attributed the statement to a media interview with a scientist who later said he had been misquoted, though the IPCC stood by its overall conclusion that “widespread mass loss from glaciers … are projected to accelerate throughout the 21st Century.”
